title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation Extension
summary: Describes a TLS extension for application-layer protocol negotiation during the handshake. When several application protocols share the same port, it lets the client and server agree which one to use.

eli5.summary: Before a conversation starts, both sides quickly agree on the language to speak. This lets a secure connection choose between protocols on one door.

questions: how does alpn work in tls
how does tls choose between http/1.1 and http/2
subtitle: How a TLS client and server agree on the application protocol, such as HTTP/1.1, during the handshake itself.

tldr.problem: Many application protocols can share one server port such as 443, and the two sides need to pick one without adding network round-trips. The server may also want to choose a certificate based on the protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The client lists its supported protocols in a TLS extension in the ClientHello, and the server answers with the one it selected in the ServerHello.
tldr.outcome: Protocol choice happens inside the existing handshake, with no extra round-trips. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8447.

today: RFC 7301 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8447. The RFC itself is not marked as obsoleted in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Negotiate the Protocol in TLS
sections.content:
Application protocols are increasingly carried inside TLS, which lets them use the secure links already present on port 443 across the global IP infrastructure. When several protocols are supported on one server-side port, the client and server must negotiate which one a given connection will use.

The RFC wants this to cost no extra network round-trips, since each round-trip degrades the user's experience. It also notes it would be useful to pick a certificate based on the negotiated protocol.

The work was requested by the HTTPbis working group to negotiate HTTP/2 over TLS, but the extension can negotiate arbitrary application-layer protocols.
sections.eli5: Lots of different programs knock on the same door. This lets the visitor say which language they speak right at the door, without making anyone walk back and forth.

sections.title: The ALPN Extension Format
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new TLS extension type, application_layer_protocol_negotiation(16), which a client MAY include in its ClientHello. Its extension_data field SHALL contain a ProtocolNameList.

Each ProtocolName is an opaque byte string of 1 to 255 bytes (ProtocolName<1..2^8-1>), and the list itself holds 2 to 65535 bytes (protocol_name_list<2..2^16-1>). The list is in descending order of preference. Empty strings MUST NOT be included and byte strings MUST NOT be truncated.

The server's reply uses the same structure, except that the list MUST contain exactly one ProtocolName.
sections.eli5: The client hands over a list of languages it can speak, favorite first. The server's answer is a list with just one language on it.

sections.title: Where ALPN Fits in the Handshake
sections.content:
Servers that receive the extension MAY return a protocol selection in a ServerHello extension of the same type. The server ignores any protocol name it does not recognize. The RFC shows both a full handshake and an abbreviated handshake carrying the extension in the ClientHello and ServerHello, so no new messages are added.

Unlike many TLS extensions, ALPN establishes properties of the connection, not of the session. When session resumption or session tickets (RFC 5077) are used, the previous contents of the extension are irrelevant and only the values in the new handshake messages are considered.
sections.eli5: The language question rides along with the greeting that happens anyway. If you come back later, you simply ask again.

sections.title: How the Server Selects a Protocol
sections.content:
A server is expected to have a list of supported protocols in preference order. It SHOULD select the most highly preferred protocol that it supports and that the client also advertised.

If the server supports none of the protocols the client advertises, it SHALL respond with a fatal no_application_protocol alert, defined as alert description 120.

The selected protocol is definitive for the connection, until renegotiated. The server SHALL NOT respond with a selected protocol and then use a different protocol for application data.
sections.eli5: The server picks the first language on the client's list that it also knows. If there is no match, it says so and hangs up.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.content:
ALPN follows the typical design of TLS extensions: the negotiation happens entirely within the client and server hello exchange. The server owns the choice, which makes it possible to base certificate selection or connection rerouting on the negotiated protocol.

The ServerHello extension is sent in plaintext so network elements can provide differentiated service when the TCP or UDP port number does not identify the application protocol. The RFC argues that negotiating in the clear avoids false confidence about hiding the protocol. If hiding is required, renegotiation after the connection is established is the preferred method.
sections.eli5: The language choice is announced out loud, so everyone knows it is not secret. If you need it secret, you decide again once the private tunnel is up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ALPN does not impact the security of TLS session establishment or application data exchange. It provides an externally visible marker for the application-layer protocol, which historically could be told from the TCP or UDP port number.

Anyone adding new protocol identifiers should remember that in TLS 1.2 and below the client sends them in the clear, and that browsers would normally use these earlier versions in the initial ClientHello for at least the next decade. If an identifier may leak personally identifiable information or enable profiling, it SHOULD NOT be used where it is visible in the clear, and the documents defining it SHOULD recommend against that use.
sections.eli5: Because the language choice is said out loud, do not pick a name that gives away private things about you.

sections.title: The Registry of Protocol IDs
sections.content:
IANA added extension type 16, application_layer_protocol_negotiation, to the ExtensionType Values registry. The RFC also creates the ALPN Protocol IDs registry, with Expert Review policy. Each entry has a protocol name, an identification sequence of octet values (which could be the UTF-8 encoding of the name) and a reference.

The initial registrations are http/1.1, spdy/1, spdy/2 and spdy/3.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of language names so everyone spells them the same way.
